usage: leafy greens sold tied together are counted in 단 (bundle), never 개
전 = a battered pan-fry; this one is the rainy-day classic
-무침 = a dish dressed by hand; a fresh, sharp 반찬 served with 삼겹살
송송 썰다 = to cut a long thin vegetable into tiny rings
examples: 부추 한 단 주세요.
One bunch of garlic chives, please.
graded simple: 한 단 is the natural market unit, not 한 개
삼겹살에는 부추무침이 잘 어울려요.
Seasoned garlic chives go really well with pork belly.
everyday: 에는 marks the topic 'as for pork belly'; 어울리다 = to suit/go with
비 오는 날엔 부추전이 딱이죠.
On a rainy day a garlic-chive pancake is just the thing.
real-situation: 딱이다 = 'is perfect/spot-on', a very natural casual close with ~죠
nuance: 부추 is the flat, soft, strongly garlic-smelling green you fold into 부추전, dress raw as 부추무침, or pack into 만두 — its flavor reads as 'garlicky onion grass', much more pungent than the mild oniony 쪽파 (thin scallion) it's often confused with at the stall. The sharpest dividing line for a learner is 부추 vs 쪽파 vs 대파: 부추 is flat and grassy, 쪽파 is a slim round-stemmed scallion, 대파 is the big leek-like green onion for stock — they are NOT interchangeable in a recipe. Register is plain everyday kitchen/market vocabulary, said freely to anyone. Big regional trap: in much of 경상도/전라도 the exact same vegetable is called 정구지, so a 시장 vendor may answer you with that word — same plant. It is sold by the 단, bruises fast, and habitually pairs with the verbs 썰다, 무치다, 부치다. English-speaker pitfall: do not reach for 'chive' as in the tiny Western garnish chive — that mental image is too delicate and too mild; 부추 is a robust cooking green, and counting it with 개 instead of 단 instantly marks you as a beginner.

usage: one bag of mung bean sprouts
packaged sprouts are counted with 봉지 (bag) at the mart
-나물 = a blanched-and-dressed vegetable side; the full proper name of 숙주 itself
데치다 = a quick scald in boiling water so they stay crunchy
tossed last into 쌀국수, 잡채, and 만두소 so they don't overcook
examples: 쌀국수에 숙주 많이 주세요.
Lots of mung bean sprouts in the pho, please.
graded simple: 많이 + 주세요 is the everyday 'give me a lot of' request
숙주는 금방 무르니까 빨리 드세요.
Mung bean sprouts go soft fast, so eat them quickly.
everyday: -니까 gives the reason; 무르다 = to go soft/mushy
숙주는 살짝만 데쳐야 아삭해요.
You have to blanch the sprouts just briefly so they stay crisp.
real-situation: -아야 = 'only if/must…'; 아삭하다 = crisp-crunchy
nuance: 숙주 (full name 숙주나물) is the slim, headless white sprout from the mung bean, and the single most important thing to lock in is the contrast 숙주 vs 콩나물: 콩나물 is the thicker soybean sprout that keeps its yellow bean head and stays firm even in soup, while 숙주 is thinner, has no visible head, tastes more delicate, and collapses quickly. At the store they sit side by side in near-identical bags, so read the label — grabbing the wrong one changes the dish. Register is plain kitchen vocabulary, neutral and used with anyone. 숙주 habitually appears with 데치다 (blanch), 무치다 (season), 넣다 (add), and lives in 쌀국수, 잡채, 비빔밥, 만두. Practical caution: it spoils within a day or two and turns slimy, so buy it the day you cook. English-speaker pitfall: 'bean sprouts' in English collapses two different Korean words into one — if you say 콩나물 expecting the pho topping you'll get the wrong, beanier sprout, and over-blanching 숙주 'to be safe' ruins exactly the crisp 아삭함 you want.

usage: leafy greens are counted in 단 (bundle); a whole 단 is the usual buy
-나물 = blanched then tossed with 참기름, 마늘, 소금; the everyday 반찬
데치다 = quick boil, then plunge into cold water to keep the green color
무치다 = to hand-mix a blanched vegetable with seasonings
examples: 시금치 한 단 주세요.
One bunch of spinach, please.
graded simple: the bare market request; counter is 단
오늘 반찬은 시금치나물이에요.
Today's side dish is seasoned spinach.
everyday: naming the day's 반찬, a very common dinner-table line
시금치는 살짝만 데쳐야 색이 안 죽어요.
You should blanch spinach just briefly so the color doesn't fade.
real-situation: 색이 죽다 = the color 'dies'/dulls — a real cook's idiom
nuance: 시금치 is leafy spinach, sold in bunches (단) and the default green for a 나물 side dish or for 잡채. The two verbs welded to it are 데치다 (blanch) then 무치다 (season) — that blanch-and-dress sequence is the master pattern for nearly every Korean leafy green, so learning it here pays off everywhere. Winter 시금치, especially the 섬초/포항초 varieties grown low to the ground, is noticeably sweeter and prized by cooks. Register is plain everyday vocabulary with no formality issues. Natural collocations: 시금치를 데치다/무치다/넣다, 시금치나물, 시금치된장국. English-speaker pitfall: spinach in the West is often eaten raw in salad, but Korean 시금치 is almost always cooked, so don't picture a raw salad green; also a classic beginner reflex is to boil it long 'until done' — over-boiling turns it dark, slippery and bitter, and counting it as 개 instead of 단 sounds off at the market. The phrase 색이 죽다 ('the color dies') is the idiomatic way cooks warn against over-blanching.

usage: counted with 개; usually sold singly, often shrink-wrapped
채 썰다 = to cut into thin matchsticks (for 호박나물/잡채)
sliced into coins, egg-battered, pan-fried; a classic 전
an almost obligatory ingredient in 된장찌개
examples: 애호박 한 개에 천오백 원이에요.
One Korean zucchini is 1,500 won.
graded simple: market price talk; counter 개 + 에 'per/for'
된장찌개에 애호박 넣을게요.
I'll put zucchini in the soybean-paste stew.
everyday: -을게요 = 'I'll (go ahead and) do it', speaker's intention
애호박을 동그랗게 썰어서 전을 부쳤어요.
I sliced the zucchini into rounds and pan-fried fritters.
real-situation: 전을 부치다 is the fixed verb for making 전, not 만들다
nuance: 애호박 is the short, pale-green, tender Korean summer squash — softer, sweeter and thinner-skinned than the dark, firm Western zucchini, which Koreans call 주키니 or 돼지호박. The contrast that matters is 애호박 vs 호박: bare 호박 leans toward pumpkin/winter squash (think 호박죽, 단호박), so if you ask for 호박 at a mart you may not get the green stew squash you pictured — say 애호박 specifically. The 애 prefix carries a 'young/tender' nuance. Register is plain everyday cooking vocabulary. It is wedded to 된장찌개, 애호박전, 호박나물, and pairs with the verbs 썰다, 채 썰다, 부치다, 넣다. English-speaker pitfall: 'zucchini' makes English speakers reach for the dark Italian kind and the all-purpose verb 만들다 for the pancake — but Korean uses the dedicated 전을 부치다 for pan-frying 전, and reaching for plain 호박 (pumpkin) instead of 애호박 is the single most common slip. Don't confuse its pale cylinder with 오이 (cucumber) either; 오이 is eaten raw and crunchy, 애호박 is cooked soft.

usage: 표고 = the most common cooking mushroom; rich aroma, meaty cap
thin white clusters; the go-to mushroom for 전골/hot pot
sold in shrink-wrapped 팩 (packs) at the mart
-볶음 = a stir-fried dish, here mushrooms with a little oil and garlic
examples: 저는 버섯을 정말 좋아해요.
I really like mushrooms.
graded simple: 을/를 좋아하다, basic preference
전골에 팽이버섯 넣으면 정말 맛있어요.
Enoki mushrooms make hot pot really tasty.
everyday: -으면 'if/when you add'; naming the specific kind, not just 버섯
표고버섯은 향이 진해서 고기 없이도 든든해요.
Shiitake has such a deep aroma it's satisfying even without meat.
real-situation: 향이 진하다 = deep scent; -아서 gives the reason
nuance: 버섯 is the umbrella word 'mushroom', but in a real kitchen or market you almost always name the kind: 표고 (shiitake, deep aroma, meaty), 팽이 (enoki, thin white clusters), 새송이 (king oyster, thick stalk), 느타리 (oyster, frilly). They're cheap, sold in 팩, and central to 전골, 샤브샤브, 불고기, and 버섯볶음. The collocation to know is 향이 진하다/좋다 ('the aroma is deep/good'), since aroma is the prized quality. Register is fully neutral. English-speaker pitfall is twofold. First, English happily lets you say just 'mushrooms' at a store, but in Korean a vendor needs the specific kind — 버섯 alone doesn't tell them whether you want 표고 or 팽이. Second is pronunciation: the final ㅅ of 버섯 is an unreleased stop [받침], pronounced like a held 't', not a clear English 's' — so it sounds closer to [버섣], and before a vowel it links (버섯이 → [버서시]). There's no Sino-Korean root here; 버섯 is a native Korean word, so don't hunt for a hanja.

usage: single leaves are counted with 장 (flat-sheet counter); a bag is 한 봉지
-장아찌 = a soy/brine pickle eaten as a 반찬
wrap (meat) in a perilla leaf and eat it
싸 먹다 = to wrap-and-eat; core 쌈 culture
its distinctive minty-anise smell — a love-it-or-not flavor for newcomers
examples: 깻잎 한 장 주세요.
One perilla leaf, please.
graded simple: 장 is the counter for flat leaves/sheets
고기를 깻잎에 싸 먹으면 더 맛있어요.
Meat tastes better wrapped in a perilla leaf.
everyday: 에 marks where you wrap; 싸 먹다 is one set verb
깻잎 향이 처음엔 좀 강할 수 있어요.
The perilla aroma can be a bit strong at first.
real-situation: -ㄹ 수 있다 = 'can/might be', a gentle hedge for newcomers
nuance: 깻잎 is the broad, jagged-edged perilla leaf eaten as a 쌈 wrap or marinated into 깻잎장아찌, and its big, polarizing minty-anise aroma is what makes it a genuine 'do you like it?' food among residents. The name is the classic trap: 깻잎 literally breaks down as 깨(sesame/perilla seed) + 잎(leaf), but it is NOT 깨 (the toasted seed you sprinkle) — same plant family, completely different ingredient and role. Don't confuse the leaf with 상추 either: 상추 is mild leaf lettuce, 깻잎 is the aromatic herb leaf, and a proper 쌈 often uses both. Register is plain everyday food vocabulary. Pronunciation is a real hurdle: 깻잎 is pronounced [깬닙] — the ㅅ받침 plus the following 이/ㅇ triggers ㄴ-insertion and nasalization, so it is NOT read letter-by-letter as [깯입]. Natural collocations: 깻잎에 싸 먹다, 깻잎장아찌, 깻잎 향, 깻잎 한 장. English-speaker pitfall: many call it 'sesame leaf' because of the 깨 in the name, but botanically it's perilla, not the sesame whose seeds you know — and saying 깨 when you mean the leaf will get you seeds, not greens.

usage: leaf lettuce is sold by the 봉지 (bag) at the mart
쌈 = a leaf-wrapped bite; the headline use of 상추
could we have some more lettuce
the standard free-refill request at a Korean BBQ table
씻다 = to rinse; you wash it leaf by leaf before wrapping
examples: 상추 한 봉지 샀어요.
I bought a bag of lettuce.
graded simple: counter 봉지 + past tense 샀어요
상추에 고기랑 마늘 올려서 싸 먹어요.
You put meat and garlic on a lettuce leaf and wrap it to eat.
everyday: 랑 = casual 'and'; 올리다 → 싸 먹다 chain explains 쌈
사장님, 상추 좀 더 주세요!
Boss, could we get some more lettuce, please!
real-situation: 사장님 = how you address the owner/server; the must-know BBQ phrase
nuance: 상추 is the soft, floppy leaf lettuce used to wrap grilled meat as 쌈 — and the sharp line to draw is 상추 vs 양배추 vs 양상추: 상추 is the tender wrapping lettuce, 양배추 is the round head cabbage, and 양상추 is crunchy iceberg/head lettuce for salads. They are different vegetables, so the 양- prefix (a 'Western/foreign' marker, as in 양파 onion, 양식 Western food) is doing real work — 상추 vs 양상추 is not just casual vs formal, it's two distinct plants. Register is plain everyday vocabulary; the only social note is the BBQ ritual phrase. The single most useful collocation a resident learns is '상추 좀 더 주세요' — refills of 상추 are free at almost every 고깃집, so this one line earns its keep nightly. Other collocations: 상추쌈, 상추를 씻다, 상추가 아삭하다/싱싱하다. English-speaker pitfall: 'lettuce' in English defaults to the crunchy salad iceberg, but 상추 is the soft wrap leaf, so don't expect a Caesar-salad crunch; and English speakers often hesitate to ask for more because in many countries refills cost extra — in Korea, just say 더 주세요. 상추 is a native Korean word, no hanja.

They are different vegetables, so the 양- prefix (a 'Western/foreign' marker, as in 양파 onion, 양식 Western food) is doing real work — 상추 vs 양상추 is not just casual vs formal, it's two distinct plants.
상추 is a native Korean word, no hanja.

'Lettuce' in English defaults to the crunchy salad iceberg, but 상추 is the soft wrap leaf, so don't expect a Caesar-salad crunch. English speakers often hesitate to ask for more because in many countries refills cost extra — in Korea, just say 더 주세요.

mistakes: Mixing up 상추 (soft wrap lettuce), 양상추 (crunchy iceberg for salad), and 양배추 (round head cabbage) — the 양- prefix marks genuinely different vegetables, not a register difference.
Not asking for refills with '상추 좀 더 주세요' — at a 고깃집 the lettuce refill is free, so it's normal and expected to ask.
Expecting iceberg-style crunch — 상추 is tender leaf lettuce meant for wrapping (쌈), not a crisp salad base.

usage: the big white radish is counted with 개; a whole one is large
반 개 = half; a normal amount to buy since a full 무 is big
채 썰다 = to cut into thin strips for 무생채/무채
a clean clear soup, often simmered with a little beef
examples: 무 반 개만 주세요.
Just half a radish, please.
graded simple: 반 개 + 만 'only', a realistic small purchase
깍두기는 무로 만든 김치예요.
Kkakdugi is kimchi made from radish.
everyday: 무로 = '(made) out of radish', instrumental 로
국 끓일 때 무를 넣으면 국물이 시원해요.
When you make soup, adding radish makes the broth clean and refreshing.
real-situation: 시원하다 here = clean/refreshing taste, NOT cold temperature
nuance: 무 is the fat, white Korean radish (daikon) — milder, juicier and far bigger than the small red Western radish, and it's the backbone of 무국, 깍두기, 동치미, 무생채, and many soup stocks. Because a whole 무 is heavy, '반 개' (half) is a perfectly normal amount to ask for. The flavor word fused to it is 시원하다: when Koreans say a 무 broth is 시원해요, they do NOT mean cold — they mean clean, brisk, and refreshing on the palate, the same 시원하다 used to praise hot soup that clears your head. Register is plain everyday vocabulary. Natural collocations: 무를 썰다/채 썰다/넣다, 무국, 무생채, 깍두기, 뭇국(소고기뭇국). English-speaker pitfall: 'radish' summons the little crunchy red salad globe, which is the wrong picture entirely — 무 is a large white root used cooked or fermented; and the 시원하다 trap is real, so a learner who hears '시원한 국' must not picture a chilled soup. 무 is a native Korean word with no hanja.

usage: 육수 = a savory stock; the base broth for many soups and 국수
-용 = 'for the purpose of'; big ones for stock vs small ones for 볶음
a sweet-savory 밑반찬 made with tiny 볶음용 anchovies
the default Korean stock combo, 멸치 + 다시마 (kelp)
examples: 멸치로 육수를 내요.
I make broth with anchovies.
graded simple: 로 = 'with/using'; 육수를 내다 is the set verb for making stock
멸치볶음은 밑반찬으로 자주 나와요.
Stir-fried anchovies often come as a standing side dish.
everyday: 밑반찬 = staple sides kept on hand; -으로 'as'
국물용 멸치는 똥을 떼고 써야 안 써요.
For broth anchovies you remove the gut before using or it turns bitter.
real-situation: 똥을 떼다 = remove the dark gut; 쓰다(bitter) puns with 쓰다(use)
nuance: 멸치 is the dried anchovy, and the practical key is that it comes in sizes by purpose: big 국물용 (broth) anchovies for making stock, and tiny 볶음용 ones for the sweet-savory 멸치볶음 side dish — the suffix -용 ('for the use of') is what tells them apart on the package. Paired with 다시마 (kelp), 멸치 forms the foundational Korean soup stock, 멸치다시마 육수, the savory base behind 국수, 떡국, 된장국 and more. Note 육수 is Sino-Korean, 肉水, literally 'meat-water' i.e. a meat/seafood stock, distinct from 물 (plain water). Register is plain kitchen vocabulary. Collocations: 육수를 내다, 멸치를 볶다, 똥을 떼다, 멸치다시마 육수. A real resident tip: pull the dark gut (똥) out of large anchovies, or the broth goes bitter. English-speaker pitfall: don't picture the oily, salty anchovy fillets from a pizza — Korean 멸치 are whole dried fish, sweet snack-sized when small and broth-makers when large; and grabbing the little snack anchovies for stock, or boiling them too long, both produce a cloudy, bitter 육수.

usage: 근 = a market unit; for meat one 근 is 600 g, not 500
the most popular cut for grilling at the table
a cheaper cut, good for 제육볶음 and stews
다짐육 = minced meat, for 만두소, 마파두부, 동그랑땡
examples: 돼지고기 한 근 주세요.
One geun (600 g) of pork, please.
graded simple: the butcher-counter line; 한 근 = 600 g
오늘 저녁은 제육볶음 해 먹을래요.
I'll make spicy stir-fried pork for dinner tonight.
everyday: -ㄹ래요 = 'I think I'll…'; 제육볶음 = spicy pork stir-fry
국거리는 돼지고기보다 소고기가 나아요.
For soup meat, beef is better than pork.
real-situation: A보다 B가 낫다 = 'B is better than A'; 국거리 = meat for soup
nuance: 돼지고기 is the everyday meat of Korea — cheaper than 소고기 (beef) and the heart of 삼겹살, 제육볶음, 김치찌개, and 보쌈. It's a transparent compound, 돼지 (pig) + 고기 (meat), and the whole 'animal + 고기' system is worth internalizing: 소고기 beef, 닭고기 chicken, 양고기 lamb. The single most practical fact is the unit: at a 정육점 (butcher) or mart, meat is sold by the 근, and for meat one 근 = 600 g — so '한 근' is noticeably more than a Western pound. (Confusingly, for vegetables/fruit a 근 is often 375 g, but for meat assume 600 g.) Register is plain everyday vocabulary. You must also learn cut names — 삼겹살 (belly), 목살 (collar/neck), 앞다리살 (shoulder), 등심 (loin) — because the butcher needs the cut, not just 'pork'. Collocations: 돼지고기 한 근, 돼지고기를 볶다/굽다/삶다, 돼지고기 다짐육. English-speaker pitfall: English 'pork' hides the animal, so beginners reach for bare 고기 (meat) — but a butcher needs to hear 돼지고기 vs 소고기; and assuming 한 근 = 500 g (or a pound) gets the quantity wrong.

Ordering 'pork' without a cut — ask by cut name (삼겹살, 목살, 앞다리살); the cut decides the dish and the price.

usage: 한 판 = a full tray of 30 eggs, the standard bulk unit at marts
single eggs are counted with 알 (counter for small round things)
spoken 계란후라이 is more common, but 프라이 is the standard spelling
풀다 here = to loosen/whisk eggs so the yolk and white blend
examples: 계란 한 판에 얼마예요?
How much is a tray of eggs?
graded simple: the mart price question; 한 판 = 30 eggs
라면에 계란 하나 풀어 드세요.
Beat an egg into your ramen and eat it.
everyday: 풀다 = whisk in; 하나 = casual 'one (egg)'
아침에 계란프라이 하나 해 먹었어요.
I made and ate a fried egg this morning.
real-situation: 해 먹다 = to cook (it) for oneself, a very common food verb
nuance: 계란 is the everyday word for 'egg' and what you'll see on most cartons, menus and lips; 달걀 is the same thing in a slightly more 'proper'/native-flavored register (often preferred in writing and textbooks), so 계란 vs 달걀 is purely register — same egg, both correct. 계란 is in fact Sino-Korean, 鷄卵, literally 'chicken-egg' (鷄 chicken + 卵 egg), which is why it can feel a touch more clinical than the native 달걀; everyday speech leans 계란. Eggs are sold by the 판 (a tray of 30) in bulk or in smaller packs, and a single egg is counted with 알 (계란 한 알). Worth pairing: 노른자 (yolk), 흰자 (white), and the verbs 풀다 (whisk), 삶다 (boil), 부치다/프라이하다 (fry). Register is fully neutral. English-speaker pitfall: learners often treat 계란 and 달걀 as two different foods or worry which is 'correct' — relax, they're interchangeable; and the counter trips people up, since eggs aren't 개 — buy them by the 판 and count singles with 알. Also note the spoken 후라이 vs written 프라이 split for the fried egg.

Counting eggs with 개 ('계란 두 개') — singles take 알 (계란 한 알), and bulk is by the 판 (tray of 30).
Writing 후라이 because that's how it sounds — the spoken 계란후라이 is normal speech, but the standard spelling is 계란프라이.

usage: the round cabbage is counted with 통 (whole-head counter)
반 통 = half; a common buy since a whole head is big
채 썰다 = to cut into thin strips for a coleslaw-style side
steamed cabbage leaves wrapped around rice/meat with 쌈장
examples: 양배추 반 통만 사고 싶어요.
I want to buy just half a head of cabbage.
graded simple: 반 통 + 만 'only'; -고 싶다 'want to'
돈가스에는 양배추 채가 같이 나와요.
Pork cutlet comes with shredded cabbage on the side.
everyday: 양배추 채 = the shredded cabbage; 같이 나오다 'comes together with'
양배추를 푹 쪄서 쌈으로 싸 먹어요.
I steam the cabbage soft and eat it as wraps.
real-situation: 푹 찌다 = steam thoroughly; 쌈으로 싸 먹다 chains the wrap idea
nuance: 양배추 is the round, dense Western-style head cabbage — and the line to nail is 양배추 vs 배추: 양배추 is the spherical green cabbage for coleslaw, 양배추쌈, and 볶음, while 배추 (specifically 배추/배추 통배추) is the tall, loose-leafed napa cabbage that becomes 김치. They are different vegetables, and the 양- prefix marks the 'Western/foreign' import (compare 양파 onion, 양상추 iceberg). It's counted with 통 (한 통 = a whole head) and very commonly bought as 반 통, since a full head is heavy. Register is plain everyday vocabulary. The signature collocation every resident meets is 돈가스 + 양배추 채 (the shredded-cabbage side with pork cutlet), plus 양배추를 찌다/볶다/채 썰다 and 양배추쌈. English-speaker pitfall: English just says 'cabbage', collapsing two Korean vegetables, so a beginner may buy round 양배추 expecting to make kimchi (which needs 배추) — getting this wrong derails the recipe; and counting it with 개 instead of 통 sounds off. 양배추 is a native-plus-Sino blend in feel but treated as a plain everyday word; no hanja drill needed.
